query: Design a lightweight alloy (<6 g/cm³) containing Magnesium and transition metals, constrained by the need to limit sintering temperature between 800 °C and 1000 °C to balance relative density and elemental volatility. The material currently suffers from unstable microstructures and poor functional properties (oxidation/corrosion) due to unclear phase transformation pathways and element segregation. Request a hypothesis on how to navigate this temperature window to form a dense, single-phase-like microstructure that maximizes barrier properties. Include prior evidence on the limitations of standard sintering in this regime, define the boundary where density fails or volatility occurs, and propose a falsification experiment comparing intermediate temperatures against the proposed optimum.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a transient liquid phase via a eutectic-forming minor alloying element (specifically 1.5 at.% Silicon) into a Mg-transition metal matrix will enable rapid densification at 850 °C, suppressing the formation of brittle intermetallic networks and element segregation that typically occur during solid-state sintering above 900 °C, thereby yielding a dense, pseudo-single-phase microstructure with enhanced oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A powder mixture of Magnesium (Mg) and a transition metal (e.g., Manganese or Zirconium) with a mean particle size of 10-20 µm, containing no intentional liquid-forming additives, currently sintered in the 800-1000 °C range resulting in porous, multiphase structures with segregated transition metal clusters.
generation.intervention: Addition of 1.5 at.% Silicon (Si) to the Mg-transition metal powder blend, followed by sintering at a precisely controlled intermediate temperature of 850 °C for 30 minutes under a high-purity Argon atmosphere with a slight overpressure to suppress Mg vaporization.
generation.conditions: Sintering temperature: 850 °C (±5 °C); Atmosphere: High-purity Argon (O2 < 10 ppm); Pressure: 1-2 MPa (if hot pressing) or standard pressure (if spark plasma sintering); Duration: 30 minutes.
generation.structural_mediator: A transient liquid phase formed by the eutectic reaction between Mg and the minor alloying element (Si), which facilitates rapid particle rearrangement and solution-precipitation kinetics while simultaneously dissolving and homogenizing the transition metal solute before solidifying into a fine, continuous matrix.
generation.mechanism: The transient liquid phase lowers the activation energy for diffusion, allowing densification to occur below the temperature where Mg volatility becomes significant (>900 °C) and where solid-state diffusion leads to coarse, unstable intermetallic precipitation. The liquid acts as a solvent for the transition metal, preventing segregation and promoting a uniform distribution that acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, effectively mimicking a single-phase microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: A relative density exceeding 98% with a homogeneous microstructure lacking large segregated intermetallic phases, resulting in a corrosion current density at least 50% lower than the baseline and a uniform oxide scale formation rate.
generation.baseline: Standard solid-state sintering of Mg-transition metal alloys at 900-950 °C, which typically yields densities <92% due to limited diffusion, accompanied by significant Mg loss (volatility) and the formation of coarse, discontinuous intermetallic networks that act as corrosion initiation sites.
generation.boundary: Density fails (porosity >5%) if the temperature is below 820 °C due to insufficient liquid formation; Volatility dominates (Mg loss >2%) if the temperature exceeds 920 °C or if the sintering time exceeds 60 minutes at 850 °C, leading to surface cracking and microstructural degradation.
generation.uncertainty: The specific eutectic composition and temperature window may vary slightly depending on the specific transition metal used (e.g., Mn vs. Zr) and the initial powder morphology; there is a risk that the transient liquid could lead to excessive grain growth if the cooling rate is not controlled, potentially negating the barrier property benefits.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of Mg-2%Mn alloys: (1) Baseline (no additive), (2) Intermediate (1.5% Si), and (3) High (2.5% Si). Sinter all sets at 800 °C, 850 °C, and 900 °C for 30 minutes. Measure density, phase composition, and corrosion rate.
measurements: Corrosion current density via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl
Mg vapor loss quantification via mass balance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the 850 °C sintered sample with 1.5% Si does not achieve a relative density >98% and a corrosion current density lower than the 900 °C baseline sample, or if the 850 °C sample shows significant Mg loss (>1%) compared to the 800 °C sample.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.
